# Mixed Effect Models in R

In this tutorial, we’ll use measurements of Galápagos finches to ask how
beak height relates to wing length. These data are available from
[BIRDD: Beagle Investigation Return with Darwinian
Data](http://bioquest.org/birdd/morph.php). These data are originally
from [Sato et al. 2000 Mol. Biol.
Evol.](http://mbe.oxfordjournals.org/content/18/3/299.full).

Each row of our dataset contains measurements from one bird, and each
taxonomic group includes observations from several individuals. We will
start by plotting the data. We will then fit a model that asks whether
taxonomic groups differ in expected beak height at a given wing length
(random intercept model). We will then fit a model to ask whether beak
height changes with wing length at different rates across groups (random
intercept and random slope model). We’ll fit and plot both models to see
what changes when we let the slopes vary by group.

## Install and load packages, download dataset

The code below will download the finch dataset from Sean Anderson's
[glmm-course github
repo](https://github.com/fall2026-skill-building-in-R/glmm-course) that
has been forked (copied) to our Skill Building in R GitHub organization.
This tutorial is based on this 2-day workshop on mixed effect models and
has lots more information on these models (and generalized linear mixed
effect models) if you are interested or need to use these models for
your research.

```{r}

# install packages if needed
if (!requireNamespace("pak", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pak")
}

pak::pak(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "lme4", "nlme", "readr", "broom.mixed"))

# load packages
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(here)
library(readr)
library(nlme)
library(lme4)
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)

# download data from GitHub
finch_file <- "Morph_for_Sato.csv"

if (!file.exists(finch_file)) {
  finch_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fall2026-skill-building-in-R/glmm-course/",
  "330571394eeb595c0e05ba5b1d282b8d003f28c7/data/raw/Morph_for_Sato.csv"
)
  finch_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(finch_url, finch_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
}

finch_raw <- read.csv(finch_file, strip.white = TRUE, na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

If downloading the data from GitHub remote did not work, use this code:

```{r}
finch_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("week-10", "tutorial", "Morph_for_Sato.csv")
) # the warning here is OK
```

## Research question, variables, and grouping

**Question.** How does beak height relate to wing length?

One row is one morphology record. Taxon is the grouping variable, as
site was in our eelgrass example. Birds in the same taxon share
biological characteristics and may be more similar than birds from
different taxa.

**Response.** beak height (mm). Predictor: wing length (mm). **Grouping
variable.** original taxon label (includes some subspecies labels).

Our first step is to wrangle our dataset. We need to trim the taxon
labels and ensure the measurements used on the log scale are positive.

```{r}

glimpse(finch_raw)

names(finch_raw) <- tolower(names(finch_raw))

finch_raw <- finch_raw |>
  dplyr::select(islandid, taxonorig, genusl69, speciesl69, sex, wingl, beakh, ubeakl) |>
  dplyr::rename(taxon = taxonorig, genus = genusl69, species = speciesl69)

finch_raw <- data.frame(na.omit(finch_raw)) # remove all rows with any NAs to make this simple

finch_raw <- dplyr::filter(finch_raw, genus == "Geospiza") |>
	as_tibble()

d <- finch_raw

glimpse(d)
```

# Initial plotting

The first rule of any data analysis is to plot the data. It's a common
saying that this is also the second and third rule of data analysis.
Never underestimate the value of plotting the data creatively.
Occasionally, we fit statistical models in between plotting the data.

We are going to look at predicting the height of birds' beaks based on
their measured wing length. And we have measurements for a variety of
species.

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(wingl, beakh, colour = taxon)) + geom_point()
```

We could fit a model to these data as they are plotted here but we might
want to consider transforming our predictor variable (wing length)
and/or our response variable (beak height).

Log transformations (using either base 10 or natural logs) are commonly
used when variables such as wing length and beak height scale
proportionally, when measurements are right-skewed, or when a
relationship looks curved on the original scale. Logging compresses
larger values more than smaller ones and can make a relationship easier
to model with a straight line.

Let's plot our data with that transformation:

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(
  log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon)) + # exercise
  geom_point()
```

One option would be to fit a single linear regression to these data. We
can quickly do that from within ggplot2 (good to just visualize, won't
give you any information other than drawing a line). Let's look at what
that would look like:

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh))) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = taxon)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") # method = [l]inear [m]odel
```

Notice that I moved `aes(colour = taxon)` within the function
`geom_point`. If I do not do that, we get a separate regression line for
each taxon, each with its own intercept and slope estimated from that
taxon’s birds.

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

Neither of these approaches is probably ideal. Why is that?

One line for all birds (complete pooling) assumes every taxon has the
same expected beak height at a given wing length. That can hide real
differences among taxa.

A separate line for each taxon (no pooling) estimates each intercept and
slope using only that taxon’s birds. For a taxon with just a few birds
or a narrow range of wing lengths, the fitted line can be unstable.

# Mixed effect model with a random intercept

## Fitting the model

A better approach might be to use a mixed effects model. Let's work
through that. We are going to use the `{lme4}` package as our default
option for fitting these types of models. Later we will explore other
packages.

Let's start from the regression syntax we already know.

```{r}
m_pooled <- lm(log(beakh) ~ log(wingl), data = d)
coef(m_pooled)
```

Now we are going to fit a mixed effects model where we let each taxon
have its own intercept. And we will constrain those different intercepts
by a normal distribution so that information is partially shared across
taxa (partial pooling).

This is often referred to as a "random intercept" model.

The workhorse function of the `{lme4}` package for fitting mixed effects
models is the function `lmer()`. You can pronounce it however you like.
Some people would say "lemur", others "ell-em-ee-are". The syntax is
just like `lm` with the addition of a formula for the "random effects".

You can find extensive details in the documentation `?lme4::lmer`.

In the code below, notice the addition `+ (1 | taxon)`. The `1` refers
to "intercept" and the `| taxon` tells the function that you want to let
the intercept vary by the values in the `taxon` column.

```{r}
m_intercept <- lme4::lmer(
  log(beakh) ~ log(wingl) + (1 | taxon),
  data = d)

summary(m_intercept)
```

## Interpreting the output

Let's read the summary together.

The summary tells us that we fit a 'Linear mixed models fit by REML' and
that the class of the object is \['lmerMod'\]. It also reports the
forumla we fit and the data.

We then have `REML criterion at convergence: -3656.1` which is the final
value of the criterion lmer() minimized to estimate the random-effect
and residual variances. It has no useful standalone interpretation as a
measure of model fit (could compare like AIC but we just use AIC).

We then have `Scaled residuals:` which is just like the `lm()`.

Next, we have a new section, `Random effects:`. This section tells us
how much variation there is among groups and how much remains within
groups. In our model, it shows how much the taxa’s fitted lines are
shifted up or down and how much individual birds scatter around their
own taxon’s line. You can take the square root of the variance column
and it equals the Std. Dev. column.

Here, the standard deviation (SD) of our taxon intercept = 0.225. At the
same wing length, a taxon’s expected log beak height typically differs
from the overall fitted line by about 0.225 log units. This describes
how much the taxon lines shift up or down.

The residual SD = 0.065. An individual bird’s log beak height typically
differs from its own taxon’s fitted line by about 0.065 log units. This
describes how much birds scatter around their taxon line.

These results tell us that the random intercept captures substantial
variation in expected beak height among taxa, even after accounting for
wing length because the taxon SD and residual SD values are not close to
zero. If the taxon intercept SD were close to zero, the model would be
estimating very little difference among taxa at the same wing length.
The taxon-specific lines would nearly overlap, so the random intercept
would add little to the fitted predictions. To see if you need a random
intercept (or both random intercept and slope) fitting a model with and
without these random effects and comparing via AIC is the best way to
judge.

We then have our `Fixed effects:` section, which gives us the estimated
intercept and slope for the overall fitted line. The intercept is the
expected log beak height at the reference wing length. The slope is the
estimated change in log beak height for a one-unit increase in log wing
length. In this random-intercept model, all taxa share that slope.

We are also told how many rows of data we have `Number of obs: 1434` and
how many random intercept groups we have `taxon, 15`.

Finally, the `Correlation of Fixed Effects:` examines the correlation
between the slope and intercept. Our model shows a very high
correlation. This isn't great, and if this correlation is very strong
and our model is complicated it might result in computational problems.
Later we will talk about ways of solving this (hint: we'll "center" the
predictor by subtracting the mean).

We can use functions in the `{lme4}` package to get the fixed and random
effect sizes:

```{r}

lme4::fixef(m_intercept)

intercept <- lme4::fixef(m_intercept)[["(Intercept)"]]
exp(intercept)

lme4::ranef(m_intercept) # gives the estimated random intercept adjustment for each taxon

coef(m_intercept) # gives you total intercept (global/population + group-level added)
# notice the slope is the same!

```

Let's make some plots of these random intercepts.

```{r}
 # row.names(.) means the row names of the data frame:
re <- lme4::ranef(m_intercept)$taxon |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "taxon") |>
  dplyr::rename(intercept_adjustment = `(Intercept)`)

ggplot(re, aes(x = 1, y = intercept_adjustment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Taxon intercept adjustment (log units)")
```

What is the mean of these random intercepts?

```{r}
round(mean(lme4::ranef(m_intercept)$taxon[, 1]), 2)
```

The mean is 0 because the random intercepts are adjustments around the
overall intercept. The overall intercept sets the baseline, and each
taxon’s adjustment shifts its line up or down from there.

There are a lot of details in the output from `summary.merMod` and
usually a lot more decimal places than are reasonable.

A useful alternative is the function `arm::display` which focuses on the
important pieces.

```{r}
arm::display(m_intercept)
```

I tend not to load the package arm, and instead call its functions
directly (e.g. `arm::display`) because the package loads many other
functions and packages that we don't need.

## Plotting the predictions

Let's look at what we just did. We'll start by plotting the predictions.
To do that, we'll use the `predict` function. Because we are applying it
to an object of class `merMod` (meaning it was created by the `lmer`
function), we can get details on that function at `?predict.merMod`.

```{r}
d$predict_lmer <- predict(m_intercept)
```

Now let's plot those predictions:

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) + # alpha = 0.1 make 10% opaque
  geom_line(aes(y = predict_lmer))
```

What do you notice about the intercepts? What do you notice about the
slopes? How does this compare to the previous 2 models we fit?

There is another kind of prediction we can make with a mixed effects
model. We can make a prediction at the "global" or "population" level.
This is our expectation if we sampled a new taxon of unknown identity.
With the lme4 package, we can do that by adding the argument
`re.form = NA` to the `predict` function:

```{r}
d$predict_lmer_population <- predict(m_intercept, re.form = NA)
```

Let's add the population prediction to the plot in black with a thicker
line:

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict_lmer)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict_lmer_population), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) 
```

## Model diagnostics

Let's inspect the model.

We can use the following code like we did with linear models, but it
only gives us the residual vs. fitted plots:

```{r}
plot(m_intercept)
```

Let's dive deeper:

First, let’s look for patterns in the residuals and check whether their
spread changes. We will plot the residuals against **fitted log beak
height** to check whether their spread changes across predicted values.
Then we’ll plot the residuals against **log wing length** to see whether
the model systematically overpredicts or underpredicts beak height at
certain wing lengths.

Each point is one bird. Its residual is its observed log beak height
minus the value predicted by its taxon’s fitted line. In both plots,
look for points scattered around zero with roughly constant vertical
spread. A curve suggests a pattern the model missed, while a fan shape
suggests changing residual variance.

```{r}
finch_diagnostics <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(m_intercept),
  residual = residuals(m_intercept),
  log_wing = model.frame(m_intercept)[["log(wingl)"]]
)

ggplot(finch_diagnostics, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted log beak height", y = "Residual")

ggplot(finch_diagnostics, aes(x = log_wing, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Log wing length", y = "Residual")
```

In both plots, the residuals are mostly scattered around zero, with no
obvious overall curve. That suggests the model isn’t consistently
overpredicting or underpredicting beak height across the range of fitted
values or wing lengths.

The spread looks somewhat wider in the middle, especially around fitted
log beak heights of 2.4–2.6. There are also more birds in that range, so
I’d describe this as a possible difference in residual spread.

Now, let's inspect the q-q plot:

```{r}
ggplot(finch_diagnostics, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line()
```

Most birds’ residuals follow the line fairly closely, so the normal
distribution describes the middle of the residual distribution
reasonably well. At the ends, some birds’ beak heights are farther from
their predicted values than we’d expect under the model’s normality
assumption.

## Next steps

What may want to consider a few things:

So far, we’ve given each taxon its own intercept and used the same slope
for all taxa. We can also let the slope vary so that the relationship
between wing length and beak height can be steeper in some taxa than in
others.

One option is a fixed-effect interaction (taxon \* log(wingl)), which
estimates each taxon’s slope using only its own observations. Another is
a random-slope model (log(wingl) + (1 + log(wingl) \| taxon)), which
uses partial pooling. Taxa with less information about their slopes tend
to have estimates closer to the overall slope. The choice depends on
your research question and how much information you have to estimate a
separate slope for each taxon.

Both approaches let the relationship between wing length and beak height
differ among taxa. The choice is how you want to estimate those
differences.

- Fixed-effect interaction (taxon \* log(wingl)) makes sense when your
  question is about specific taxa and you have enough birds across a
  useful range of wing lengths in each taxon. For example, “How much
  steeper is the slope for G. fortis than for G. scandens?” Each taxon’s
  slope is estimated from its own observations.

- Random slopes (log(wingl) + (1 + log(wingl) \| taxon)) make sense when
  you want to estimate the overall slope and how much slopes vary among
  taxa. The model also gives each taxon its own slope estimate. Through
  partial pooling, a taxon with only a few birds or a narrow range of
  wing lengths generally gets an estimate closer to the overall slope.
  If you have taxa with few data points, you'd want to consider fitting
  random intercepts and slopes to help estimate the effect sizes for
  data-poor taxa.

We might also want to try centering the predictor to reduce correlation
between the intercept and slope and make the intercept more
interpretable.

## Using {nlme}

Here is a quick example of fitting the same random-intercept model in
the other common mixed-effects modeling package:

```{r}
m_intercept_nlme <- nlme::lme(
  log(beakh) ~ log(wingl),
  random = ~ 1 | taxon,
  data = d,
  method = "REML"
)

tibble::tibble(
  term = names(lme4::fixef(m_intercept)),
  lme4 = unname(lme4::fixef(m_intercept)),
  nlme = unname(nlme::fixef(m_intercept_nlme))
)

nlme::VarCorr(m_intercept_nlme)
```

Let's compare predictions from the two packages:

```{r}
prediction_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(
    type = "Global (or population) predictions",
    lme4 = predict(m_intercept, newdata = d, re.form = NA),
    nlme = predict(m_intercept_nlme, newdata = d, level = 0)
  ),
  tibble::tibble(
    type = "Group-level predictions",
    lme4 = predict(m_intercept, newdata = d, re.form = NULL),
    nlme = predict(m_intercept_nlme, newdata = d, level = 1)
  )
)

ggplot(prediction_comparison, aes(x = lme4, y = nlme)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~ type) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted log beak height (lme4)",
    y = "Predicted log beak height (nlme)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The predictions are the same for the global and group levels.

# Mixed effect models with a random intercept and slope

Let's plot the data to remember what they looked like.

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon)) +
  geom_point() 
```

## Fitting the model

Last time we assumed that the slopes were constant across taxa. The
above plot suggests that they might not be.

Let's modify the mixed-effects model we fit last time by allowing the
slopes to vary. In `(1 + log(wingl) | taxon)`, `1` lets each taxon have
its own intercept, and `log(wingl)` lets each taxon have its own slope.
The `log(wingl)` term outside the parentheses estimates the overall
slope, and the term inside gives each taxon an adjustment to that slope.
This model will fit a random intercept **and** a random slope. You
rarely fit a model with just a random slope.

```{r, message=FALSE}
m_int <-  lmer(log(beakh) ~ log(wingl) + (1 | taxon), data = d)
m_slopes <-  lmer(log(beakh) ~ log(wingl) + (1 + log(wingl) | taxon), data = d)
```

## Interpreting the output

Let's look at the output from those two models.

```{r}
arm::display(m_int)
arm::display(m_slopes)

AIC(m_int, m_slopes)
```

In the output for the model with random intercept and random slope, we
now have a line that reads `log(wingl)`. This is the standard deviation
(SD) of the random slopes, meaning that the taxon-specific slopes vary
around the population-level slope of 1.01 with a SD of 0.31. This means
95% of taxon slopes will be 1.96 \* SD + - 1.01 (\~0.4 to 1.62; the
actual range is 0.67 to 1.49, so narrower than CIs).

## Plotting the predictions

We can make predictions just like before.

```{r}
d$predict_int <- predict(m_int)
d$predict_slopes <- predict(m_slopes)
```

We'll plot the random intercept predictions in `"grey"` and the random
intercept and slope predictions in `"black"`.

```{r}
ggplot(d, aes(log(wingl), log(beakh), colour = taxon, group = taxon)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict_int), colour = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict_slopes), colour = "black") 
```

## Model diagnostics

Let's extract residuals, predictions, and fitted values from the model
objects using the `broom.mixed::augment` functions.

```{r}
aug_int <- broom.mixed::augment(m_int)
aug_slopes <- broom.mixed::augment(m_slopes)
head(aug_slopes)
```

One important model diagnostic is plotting the residuals against the
fitted values. Here, "fitted" is another word for the predictions.

We'll start with the random intercepts model and plot by taxon:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(aug_int, aes(.fitted, .resid)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + 
  facet_wrap(~taxon, scales = "free") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2)
```

Is there anything concerning with the above plot? Hint: Look for curves
or changes in spread of points.

And now, the random intercepts and slopes model:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(aug_slopes, aes(.fitted, .resid)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + 
  facet_wrap(~taxon, scales = "free") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2)
```

This looks a bit better. Why is that? But there are still some problems.
The biggest issue, to me, is the curve that we see for *Geospiza
fortis*:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
filter(aug_slopes, taxon == "Geospiza fortis") %>%
  ggplot(aes(.fitted, .resid)) + geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)
```

How might we fix this? Hint: think back to last week!

## Using {nlme}

```{r}
m_slopes_nlme <- nlme::lme(
  fixed = log(beakh) ~ log(wingl),
  random = ~ 1 + log(wingl) | taxon,
  data = d,
  method = "REML"
)
```

# Mixed effect models with a gam()

Now let’s fit a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM). We’ll replace
the overall straight line with a smooth and see how taxon-specific
intercepts and slopes let each taxon shift and tilt that curve. We’ll
use `gam()` and `gamm()` from `{mgcv}`. The `{gamm4}` package is another
option. Here we are going to center the predictor (wing length).

```{r}
# ungroup data frame and make taxon a factor
d_gamm <- d |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(taxon = factor(taxon)) |>
	mutate(log_wingl_centered = log(wingl) - mean(log(wingl)))

## fit a generalized additive mixed effects model (GAMM) using gam():

# random intercept only
m_gamm_int <- mgcv::gam(
  log(beakh) ~ s(log_wingl_centered, k = 10) +
    s(taxon, bs = "re"),
  data = d_gamm,
  method = "REML"
)

# random intercept and separate curve (with shared curvature) by group:
m_gamm_slope <- mgcv::gam(
  log(beakh) ~ s(log_wingl_centered, k = 10) +
    s(taxon, bs = "re") +
    s(taxon, log_wingl_centered, bs = "re"),
  data = d_gamm,
  method = "REML"
)


## fit a generalized additive mixed effects model (GAMM) using gamm():

# Shared smooth with a random intercept for taxon
m_gamm_pkg_int <- mgcv::gamm(
  log(beakh) ~ s(log_wingl_centered, k = 10),
  random = list(taxon = ~ 1),
  data = d_gamm,
  method = "REML"
)

# Shared smooth with taxon-specific intercept and slope adjustments
m_gamm_pkg_slope <- mgcv::gamm(
  log(beakh) ~ s(log_wingl_centered, k = 10),
  random = list(taxon = ~ 1 + log_wingl_centered),
  data = d_gamm,
  method = "REML"
)
```

Fitting GAMMs in `gam()` and `gamm()` let each taxon shift and tilt the
shared curve. In our `gam()` model, the two separate `bs = "re"` terms
assume that the intercept and slope adjustments are uncorrelated. In our
`gamm()` model, `random = list(taxon = ~ 1 + log_wingl_centered)`
estimates that correlation. It tells us whether taxa with taller
predicted beaks at the reference wing length tend to have steeper or
shallower slopes at that point.

## Predictions

```{r}
# create a prediction grid for each taxon
gamm_predictions <- d_gamm |>
  dplyr::group_by(taxon) |>
  dplyr::reframe(
    log_wingl_centered = seq(
      from = min(log_wingl_centered),
      to = max(log_wingl_centered),
      length.out = 100
    )
  )

# add the predicted beak height from both models back into gamm_predctions:
gamm_predictions$random_intercept_mod <- predict(
  m_gamm_int, newdata = gamm_predictions, type = "response"
)

gamm_predictions$random_intercept_slope_mod <- predict(
  m_gamm_slope, newdata = gamm_predictions, type = "response"
)

# plot
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = d_gamm,
    aes(x = log_wingl_centered, y = log(beakh)),
    alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(
    data = gamm_predictions,
    aes(log_wingl_centered, random_intercept_mod, colour = "Random intercept"),
    linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(
    data = gamm_predictions,
    aes(log_wingl_centered, random_intercept_slope_mod,
        colour = "Random intercept + slope"),
    linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ taxon, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Random intercept" = "#0072B2",
    "Random intercept + slope" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Centered log wing length", y = "Log beak height", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Model diagnostics

```{r}
# shared smooth with taxon random intercepts
gratia::appraise(m_gamm_int, type = "response")

# shared smooth with taxon random intercepts and slopes
gratia::appraise(m_gamm_slope, type = "response")

mgcv::k.check(m_gamm_int)
mgcv::k.check(m_gamm_slope)
```

We allowed `k = 10` in our GAMMs. Our k-index values are below that
target value of 1, meaning that individuals with similar wing lengths
tend to have more similar residuals than expected. This may be due to
phylogenetic relatedness rather than model fit. Phylogenetic models are
very advanced and we won't go into them here. If you are curious, see
[the brms package
vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/brms/vignettes/brms_phylogenetics.html).

We also want to check the residuals vs. fitted of the species that had a
curved pattern when fitting a linear mixed effect model:

```{r}
# m_slopes is the linear mixed model with a random intercept and slope.
fortis_diagnostics <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(
    taxon = model.frame(m_slopes)$taxon,
    log_wing = model.frame(m_slopes)[["log(wingl)"]],
    residual = residuals(m_slopes),
    model = "Linear mixed model"
  ),
  tibble::tibble(
    taxon = model.frame(m_gamm_slope)$taxon,
    log_wing = model.frame(m_gamm_slope)$log_wingl_centered +
      mean(log(d_gamm$wingl)),
    residual = residuals(m_gamm_slope, type = "response"),
    model = "GAMM with shared smooth"
  )
) |>
  dplyr::filter(taxon == "Geospiza fortis")

ggplot(fortis_diagnostics, aes(log_wing, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Log wing length", y = "Residual")
```

This plot looks much better.

# Next steps

GAMMs can be very complicated. Here, we allowed a random intercept and a
shared curve with group-level deviations. There are many options and
there is a nice paper by Eric Pederson, David Miller, Gavin Simpson, and
Noam Ross that explains the most commonly used options (check out Figure
4).

In our example, all taxa shared the same curvature. The random intercept
lets each taxon shift the curve up or down, and the random slope lets
each taxon tilt it. [Pedersen et al.
(2019)](https://peerj.com/articles/6876/) describe five ways to model
smooths across groups:

- **G:** One overall smooth shared by all groups.

- **GS:** An overall smooth plus group-specific smooth deviations, with
  a shared smoothing penalty.

- **GI:** An overall smooth plus group-specific smooth deviations, with
  a separate smoothing penalty for each group.

- **S:** A separate smooth for each group, with a shared smoothing
  penalty.

- **I:** A separate smooth for each group, with a separate smoothing
  penalty for each group.

A shared penalty controls how much the curves can wiggle in the same way
across groups. The curves themselves can still have different shapes.
